A Democratic Imperative for Informational Sovereignty: The Case for a Dominant, Publicly-Financed National News Service in the United States

I. The Stakes: Truth as Public Infrastructure
Every society depends on shared facts the way it depends on safe water and navigable roads. When facts are unreliable, everything downstream—public deliberation, market confidence, the legitimacy of elections—erodes. Private media once prided itself on a public-interest ethos, but the digital age severed the link between journalistic quality and financial return. The result is a cacophony optimized for outrage and clicks rather than accountability; social platforms amplify the extremes while profitable partisanship seeps into cable, talk radio, and even local newsrooms dominated by hedge funds. Poll after poll shows a majority of Americans can no longer agree on basic realities such as the integrity of the 2020 election, the safety of vaccines, or even who won the Super Bowl. A republic cannot govern itself if its citizens inhabit mutually incompatible information universes. The remedy is not more deregulation, which merely hands ever-larger megaphones to interest groups, but rather the deliberate creation of a dominant public news utility insulated from market imperatives yet fully accountable to the electorate.

II. Crafting the Institution: Design Principles for Burstiness and Operational Durability

  1. Legal Identity. Congress charters an independent United States Public News Corporation (US-PNC) as a cognate to the Federal Reserve and the Smithsonian—a “Fourth Branch service” whose budget is automatically appropriated at 0.2 % of federal outlays and shielded from annual political haggling.
  2. Governance. A thirteen-member board selected by the president from a bipartisan slate submitted by a blue-ribbon civic committee and confirmed by the Senate for staggered seven-year terms. No sitting politician, party official, or person with a substantial financial stake in any private media company may serve. Once appointed, board members may be removed only for narrowly defined cause via supermajority vote of the Supreme Court, ensuring insulation from retribution for unflattering coverage.
  3. Editorial Independence. The board sets an explicit charter (“fearless, fact-checking, and non-partisan explanatory journalism in the public interest”). An ombudsman chosen by unanimous consent of the board from among ten nominees supplied by the deans of accredited journalism schools handles complaints. All editorial decision logs (not source identities) are made public annually—bursting into view rather than buried in bureaucracy—subject to narrowly scoped national-security exemptions.
  4. Staffing & Culture. Salaries are pegged at the top 75th percentile of private broadcast journalism to recruit elite talent, with rotating three-year secondments from regional stringers, rural outlets, and trade reporters to ensure ideological and geographical variety. Public editors and adversarial fact-checkers are embedded into every newsroom cluster, their tweets, blogs, and on-air segments instantly visible—no ossified monoculture here.
  5. Revenue & Reach. The budget finances television, radio, streaming, a news-wire, and aggressive social-native content. Simulcast obligations on all major cable systems (similar to C-SPAN) and must-carry rules for over-the-air networks ensure baseline nationwide availability. All stories are released simultaneously under an unrestricted Creative Commons license to local outlets, universities, and civic tech start-ups—a backstop against algorithmic throttling.
  6. Transparency Sunlight. All raw data, anonymized interview audio, and FOIA responses, codebooks, and methodology are published on GitHub within 48 hours. A built-in API enables any developer to remix feeds into new formats—from TikTok explainers to rural low-bandwidth MMS bulletins—encouraging creative burstiness at the edges while the central outlet remains authoritative.

III. Safeguards: What Keeps the Behemoth Honest
• Annual public deliberations modeled on the Fed chair’s Humphrey-Hawkins testimony, except the US-PNC editor-in-chief faces citizens selected by lottery, CNN hosts, Breitbart livestreamers, high-school bloggers—any manner of interrogators in a televised marathon.
• Continuous external audits by universities, press associations, and civil-society groups with subpoena power over internal memos, published online in machine-readable form.
• A standing incentive: any whistle-blower inside the agency whose documented evidence leads to a substantiated finding of state-directed distortion wins a statutory bounty equal to one-year full salary—indexed for inflation—plus lifetime immunity from federal employment reprisal.

IV. Antidotes to “State Propaganda” Charges
Critics will invoke Pravda, TASS, or China Daily. The flaw in these analogues is not public ownership per se but (1) single-party control, (2) opaque budgets, and (3) zero civil scrutiny. The US-PNC blueprint inverts each vector: plural governance, hard-wired transparency, statutory whistle-blower protection, multiple overlapping audit chains, and a charter that enshrines adversarial coverage of every branch of government—including itself. Private networks, far from being muzzled, enjoy increased oxygen because the public option crowds out sensationalist clickbait with soberly sourced facts. Reporters at Fox, BuzzFeed, or TheBlaze lose nothing; they simply gain an ironclad baseline subsidy of verifiable context against which their commentary can be judged.

V. Counteracting Private Bias Through Structural Dominance

  1. Market Share Target: funded to reach 40 % of average daily news-minutes within ten years. Not monopoly, but gravity—large enough that private outlets must match its credibility or be displaced.
  2. Algorithm Compliance. Federal legislation conditions Section 230 immunities on “reasonable parity” in recommendation surfacing of any story fact-checked and cleared by the US-PNC. Platforms may still preference opinion pieces or alternative analyses, but not suppress or downgrade immutable corrections issued by the agency.
  3. Antitrust Trigger: any private media conglomerate whose audience share slips below 8 % for two consecutive quarters can re-price carriage agreements without antitrust challenge, incentivizing nimble flash-point journalism instead of rent-seeking gatekeeping.

VI. Economic & Cultural Dividends
• A domestic market less polluted by conspiracy theories reduces insurance premiums, public-health misinformation costs, and election-law litigation. A 2022 RAND study estimates direct economic losses from mis- and disinformation in the U.S. at $78 billion annually. Reclaiming even half that figure dwarfs the US-PNC’s projected $9 billion budget.
• Local news desert recovery. The universal CC-license clause means a thousand unemployed local investigative journalists can syndicate national US-PNC content while layering hyper-local angles—restoring civic glue to county fairs, school boards, and city councils.
• Restoration of professional prestige when a young Pierre Salinger Medalist chooses public service journalism over corporate public-relations or silicon-spin because a career ladder now exists that rewards truth, not TikTok virality.

VII. Concluding Indictment and Call to Action
Private media promised a marketplace of ideas yet delivered ideological black markets and algorithmic addiction. The Founders chartered a post office and subsidized newspapers by law for precisely this reason—information is not a mere commodity but the sovereign’s circulatory system. We repaired roads with the Interstate Highway Act, we tamed the banks with Glass-Steagall, and we corralled airwaves with the FCC. It is long past time we treat factual infrastructure with the same unsentimental rigor. A dominant, publicly-funded, democratically-governed news corporation is not an overreach; it is the minimal step necessary to rescue self-government from a slow-motion cognitive civil war. Congress should act now, not to silence anyone, but to guarantee that every American—left, right, north, south, wired or off-grid—can meet on common empirical ground before the next consequential election, the next pandemic, the next fateful debate the republic faces.

The Case for an American Public News Service: A Framework for Reliable, Noncommercial Journalism

Introduction

In an era defined by information warfare, algorithmic radicalization, and the fragmentation of shared factual reality, the United States faces an unprecedented crisis in public communication. Private media corporations, driven by profit motives and ideological commitments, have proven incapable of serving the informational needs of a functioning democracy. The solution lies not in regulating private media—a approach that would raise serious First Amendment concerns—but in establishing a robust, adequately funded, and genuinely independent public news service that can provide Americans with reliable, comprehensive, and unbiased news coverage. Such an institution would strengthen rather than threaten democratic discourse by offering a common factual foundation upon which citizens can make informed decisions.

The Crisis in American Journalism

The American media landscape has undergone a transformation over the past three decades that has fundamentally compromised its ability to serve the public interest. The collapse of the business model that once supported local journalism has left countless communities without access to professional news coverage. According to research from journalism schools and media watchdogs, thousands of newspapers have closed, hundreds of newsrooms have shrunk, and entire regions of the country have become "news deserts" where citizens have no access to local reporting on their schools, governments, and civic institutions.

This collapse has not merely reduced the quantity of news available; it has degraded the quality of the news that remains. Surviving media organizations, facing declining revenues and intense pressure from corporate owners, have increasingly turned to sensationalism, partisan commentary, and clickbait journalism to attract audiences in a fragmented media marketplace. The result is a public discourse characterized by outrage, polarization, and mutual incomprehension rather than informed deliberation about genuine policy choices.

Meanwhile, the rise of social media as a primary news source for many Americans has created an environment in which misinformation spreads rapidly and widely, while accurate information struggles to compete with emotionally provocative content. Private platforms have demonstrated either inability or unwillingness to address this problem effectively, prioritizing engagement metrics over factual accuracy and allowing bad actors—foreign and domestic—to exploit their networks for purposes of manipulation and division.

The Failure of Private Solutions

Critics of public media often argue that the marketplace of ideas, left to its own devices, will eventually sort truth from falsehood and that government involvement in journalism represents a dangerous step toward authoritarianism. This argument, however, ignores the abundant evidence that marketplace dynamics in contemporary media do not reward accuracy and nuance but rather emotional intensity and tribal affiliation.

Private media corporations have explicit editorial agendas, whether acknowledged or not. These agendas reflect the political preferences of corporate owners, the ideological commitments of editorial staff, and the commercial imperative to cater to existing audience preferences rather than challenge them. The result is a media environment in which citizens can easily find confirmation of whatever they already believe but struggle to encounter information that might complicate or revise their worldview. This dynamic has contributed significantly to political polarization and the inability of Americans to agree even on basic facts.

Furthermore, the concentration of media ownership in the hands of a few large corporations raises serious concerns about the diversity of perspectives available to the public. When a handful of companies control the major broadcast networks, cable news channels, and large newspaper chains, the range of viewpoints that reach most Americans is necessarily limited by the editorial preferences and commercial interests of those owners. This concentration has accelerated in recent years as private equity firms and billionaire media moguls have acquired struggling news organizations, often to advance political agendas or protect business interests.

The Case for Public Service Journalism

A properly designed public news service would address these failures by providing journalism that is independent of both commercial pressures and partisan political control. Such an institution would be dedicated not to maximizing profit or advancing a particular ideological agenda but to informing the American public with the maximum possible accuracy, comprehensiveness, and fairness.

The model for such an institution exists in the form of public broadcasting systems in other democratic nations. The British Broadcasting Corporation, for example, has for nearly a century provided news coverage that is widely respected for its accuracy and impartiality, despite being funded by a license fee collected from households that use television receivers. Similarly, Canada's CBC/Radio-Canada, Japan's NHK, and public broadcasting systems in Germany and throughout Europe have demonstrated that noncommercial, publicly funded journalism can thrive and serve democratic values even in an era of intense media competition.

These international examples demonstrate that public media can maintain independence from governmental interference while serving the public interest. Crucially, this independence depends not on ideological commitments to neutrality but on institutional structures that insulate editorial decisions from political pressure. Board structures with staggered terms, secure funding mechanisms that cannot be manipulated through annual appropriations, and strong editorial independence guarantees have allowed public broadcasters in other democracies to maintain credibility even in highly polarized political environments.

Addressing the Objections

Critics of public media in the United States raise several legitimate concerns that must be addressed directly. The most fundamental objection is that any government involvement in journalism threatens freedom of the press and creates a slippery slope toward authoritarian control. This objection deserves serious consideration, but it rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of the distinction between government control of media and government support for journalism.

The First Amendment was designed to prevent the government from suppressing speech or controlling what private citizens and organizations can publish. It does not prohibit the government from establishing its own communications or from supporting journalism that serves the public interest. Indeed, the federal government has long supported various forms of communication, from the Postal Service to public libraries to the Congressional Research Service, without these activities being considered threats to free speech.

A properly designed public news service would be independent of governmental control in its editorial decisions. Its funding would be secure and its governance structure would include mechanisms to prevent political interference. This is not utopian idealism; it is the model that has worked successfully in democracies around the world for generations. The question is not whether government can be trusted with media—private media corporations are already trusted with enormous influence over public discourse—but whether institutional design can create structures that serve the public interest.

Another objection concerns the potential for public media to become a tool for propaganda or ideological manipulation. This concern is understandable given the history of state-controlled media in authoritarian regimes, but it fails to distinguish between genuinely independent public media and propaganda organs. The key difference lies in institutional independence, editorial autonomy, and transparency about processes and standards. Public media in democratic nations maintain credibility precisely because they have established processes for ensuring accuracy and fairness, including ombudsman offices, editorial boards with diverse perspectives, and correction policies that acknowledge and remedy errors.

The Practical Benefits

A robust public news service would provide concrete benefits that private media cannot or will not deliver. First, it would address the crisis in local journalism by investing in reporting on state and local governments, school boards, city councils, and other institutions that affect citizens' daily lives but have lost coverage as local newspapers have declined. This "accountability journalism" is essential for democratic governance at all levels, yet the market has proven incapable of supporting it.

Second, a public news service would provide comprehensive coverage of national and international affairs that private media, focused on maximizing audience and revenue, increasingly neglect. Foreign bureaus have been eliminated, investigative journalism has declined, and coverage has become increasingly superficial and sensational. A public service with a mandate to inform rather than entertain would invest in the kind of journalism that democracies need but markets cannot support.

Third, such an institution would provide a common source of information that could serve as a shared foundation for public discourse. In an era when different Americans get their news from radically different sources with competing claims about basic facts, a respected public news service could help restore the shared reality that democratic deliberation requires. This does not mean that everyone would agree about interpretation or policy, but it would mean that disagreements would be grounded in agreement about what is actually happening.

Fourth, a public news service would be better positioned than private media to counter misinformation and foreign influence operations. With resources for verification, fact-checking, and rapid response to false claims, and without the commercial pressures that sometimes lead private media to amplify sensational or false information for clicks, a public news service could serve as a trusted source of accurate information in an environment where trust is scarce.

Institutional Design Considerations

The success of any American public news service would depend crucially on its institutional design. Several principles should guide this design to ensure genuine independence and public credibility.

Funding should be secure and not subject to annual appropriations that could be used as leverage for political interference. Several models exist internationally, from license fees (which raise constitutional concerns in the American context) to dedicated funding streams protected from political manipulation. The exact mechanism is less important than the outcome: a funding structure that allows the institution to plan and operate independently of political pressure.

Governance should include mechanisms to ensure diversity of perspective and to insulate editorial decisions from political control. Board members should have staggered terms, selection processes that include diverse stakeholders, and clear mandates for editorial independence. Editorial decisions should be made by professional journalists according to professional standards, not by board members or government officials.

Transparency should be built into every aspect of operations. Corrections should be prompt and prominent. Sources and methodology should be disclosed where possible. Editorial processes should be documented and available for public review. This transparency is the foundation of credibility in an era when trust in institutions has declined.

The scope of coverage should be comprehensive but distinct from private media. Rather than competing for sports, entertainment, or celebrity coverage, a public news service should focus on the journalism that private markets undersupply: investigative reporting, foreign coverage, local accountability journalism, and in-depth analysis of complex issues. This specialization would allow public and private media to complement rather than compete with each other.

Conclusion

The crisis in American journalism is real, and its consequences for democratic governance are serious. Private media, driven by commercial imperatives and ideological commitments, has proven incapable of providing the information that citizens need to govern themselves effectively. The solution is not to regulate or constrain private media—which would raise serious constitutional and practical concerns—but to establish a robust public alternative that can provide the journalism democracy requires.

The experience of other democracies demonstrates that publicly funded, independent journalism can thrive and can earn the trust of citizens even in highly polarized political environments. The question for Americans is whether they have the institutional creativity to design such a system for their own context. The answer should be yes, because the stakes are too high to accept the status quo.

A well-designed public news service would strengthen American democracy by providing reliable information, supporting accountability at all levels of government, and offering a shared foundation for public discourse. It would not replace private media but would complement it, filling the gaps that commercial pressures have created. Most importantly, it would affirm the principle that information is a public good deserving public support—that in a democracy, an informed citizenry is not merely a commercial product but a constitutional requirement.

The time to act is now, before the collapse of local journalism becomes irreversible, before misinformation completely supplants shared factual reality, before the fragments of American discourse become so scattered that no common conversation remains. Establishing a strong, independent, adequately funded public news service is not a step toward authoritarianism but a bulwark against it—an affirmation that democratic self-governance requires citizens who are informed, engaged, and capable of deliberating together about their common future.

Arguments for a State-Run News Organization in the United States: A Balanced Examination

The proposition of establishing a major state-run, government-controlled news organization in the United States represents one of the most debated topics in American media policy. While such an idea runs counter to long-standing traditions of private media ownership and First Amendment protections that define American journalism, proponents advance several theoretical benefits worth examining. This analysis explores the arguments made by advocates while acknowledging the significant counterarguments and challenges such a proposal would face.

Theoretical Benefits and Proposed Advantages

Addressing Commercial Media Failures

Advocates for a state-run news organization frequently argue that commercial media's profit-driven model produces systematic failures in public information. Under the current system, media outlets must maximize advertising revenue, which creates incentives for sensationalism, clickbait, and coverage that prioritizes entertainment over substance. A publicly funded organization without commercial pressures, proponents contend, could prioritize in-depth investigative journalism, complex policy analysis, and long-form explanatory reporting that rarely generates sufficient clicks or ratings to justify private investment.

The economic pressures facing local journalism provide particularly compelling evidence for reform advocates. As newspapers have declined, thousands of communities have lost their only local news source, creating "news deserts" where residents have limited access to information about local government, schools, and civic affairs. A state-run organization could theoretically establish bureaus in underserved areas, ensuring that all Americans have access to reliable local news regardless of the commercial viability of their market.

Reducing Perceived Partisan Bias

The fragmentation of the American media landscape into ideologically aligned outlets has led many citizens to perceive bias across the spectrum. Some argue that a professionally managed public news organization, governed by independent boards and subject to rigorous editorial standards, could provide coverage that transcends partisan framing. The BBC in the United Kingdom, while not without its critics, demonstrates that state-run broadcasting can achieve broad public trust and maintain editorial independence in certain democratic contexts.

Proponents suggest that such an organization could establish clear standards for factual reporting, distinguish clearly between news and opinion, and provide balanced coverage of controversial issues. By investing in professional journalism education and fact-checking infrastructure, a public news service might establish benchmarks for accuracy that private outlets would have incentives to follow, potentially elevating standards across the entire media ecosystem.

Serving National Information Needs

Advocates argue that certain types of coverage serve essential national interests but receive inadequate attention from commercial media. National security reporting, diplomatic affairs, climate science, and public health information all require significant resources and expertise that private outlets may hesitate to invest in during periods of financial constraint. A state-run organization could maintain specialized correspondent networks in Washington, D.C., international capitals, and scientific centers, providing expertise that few private organizations can afford.

During national emergencies—whether pandemics, natural disasters, or security threats—proponents contend that a coordinated public information effort could save lives and ensure citizens receive accurate, timely guidance. The fragmented nature of American media during such events can lead to confusion, misinformation, and inconsistent messaging that a unified public service could potentially avoid.

Promoting Media Literacy and Civic Education

Some proponents emphasize the educational potential of a public news organization. Beyond daily news coverage, such an entity could develop programming specifically designed to help citizens understand complex policy issues, evaluate sources critically, and navigate an increasingly complex information environment. Explainers on how government works, interactive tools for understanding data, and educational content for schools could all serve democratic education goals that commercial media has limited incentive to pursue.

This educational mission could extend to training the next generation of journalists, offering fellowships and internships that develop professional skills while instilling ethical standards and commitment to public service journalism.

Significant Challenges and Counterarguments

Constitutional and Cultural Barriers

Any proposal for government-controlled news in America confronts the fundamental tension with First Amendment traditions that have defined American journalism for over two centuries. The constitutional protection of press freedom reflects a philosophical commitment that government should not control or significantly influence the flow of information to citizens. Creating a major state-run news organization would require navigating these constitutional protections, potentially raising significant legal challenges regarding government speech, public forum doctrine, and editorial independence.

Beyond legal questions, American political culture has historically viewed government involvement in media with deep suspicion. Unlike European nations where public broadcasting developed alongside different constitutional traditions, American skepticism about government power extends to skepticism about government information services. This cultural barrier means any such proposal would face significant political opposition and require extraordinary measures to establish public credibility.

The Problem of Government Influence

The central paradox of state-run media concerns the relationship between government funding and editorial independence. Even with structural safeguards designed to protect autonomy, critics argue that government-funded entities inevitably face pressure—overt or subtle—to avoid coverage that embarrasses administrations or challenges powerful interests. The dependence on congressional appropriations creates vulnerability to political retaliation that would compromise editorial judgment.

International examples of state-run media offer sobering lessons. While the BBC maintains strong independence, many state-run broadcasters around the world serve as propaganda organs for ruling parties. Even in well-functioning democracies, public broadcasters have faced political pressure during controversies involving government conduct. Proponents argue that American institutional safeguards could prevent such outcomes, but skeptics point out that these same safeguards have proven insufficient to prevent polarization and politicization in other government institutions.

Competitive Distortion Concerns

Critics argue that a state-run news organization would distort the media marketplace in ways that harm rather than help public information. Government subsidies would create unfair competition for private outlets already struggling with declining revenue. Rather than elevating standards, a well-funded public competitor might accelerate the decline of private journalism, reducing the diversity of voices and perspectives in the media ecosystem.

Furthermore, the existence of an official government news source might actually reduce civic engagement by providing a single "authorized" perspective that citizens treat as definitive, potentially discouraging the critical evaluation and diverse viewpoints that a healthy democracy requires.

Existing Alternatives and Institutional Capacity

The United States already possesses significant public media infrastructure through PBS, NPR, and various state-level public broadcasting entities. These organizations demonstrate both the potential and limitations of non-commercial, publicly supported journalism in America. Rather than creating an entirely new government-controlled entity, reformers might argue for expanding and protecting these existing institutions.

Additionally, proposals for government-controlled news face practical questions about institutional capacity and implementation. Building a major news organization requires not just funding but journalistic talent, institutional culture, and public trust—assets that cannot be created through legislation but must be earned over decades of reliable service.

Conclusion: A Contested Vision

The proposal for a major state-run news organization in America reflects genuine concerns about the failures of contemporary media and the health of democratic discourse. The arguments advanced by proponents—that commercial pressures degrade information quality, that partisan fragmentation undermines shared understanding, and that certain public interest journalism requires sustained investment that private markets cannot provide—deserve serious consideration rather than dismissal.

However, these theoretical benefits must be weighed against the substantial risks of government influence over information, the constitutional and cultural barriers to implementation, and the potential for such an organization to harm rather than help the media ecosystem it seeks to improve. The American tradition of privately owned, editorially independent journalism has produced both remarkable journalism and significant problems—a complex legacy that any reform proposal must honestly confront.

Ultimately, the debate over state-run news organization reflects deeper questions about the role of government in democratic society, the nature of reliable information, and the institutional arrangements best suited to sustaining an informed citizenry. These questions lack simple answers, and the proposed solutions carry significant trade-offs that citizens and policymakers must carefully consider.

While private media theoretically serves public interests through competition, market forces have steered journalism away from its civic purpose. The profit motive incentivizes sensationalism over substance, conflict over clarity, and speed over accuracy. As media scholar Robert McChesney notes, "What is good for the bottom line of media corporations is not necessarily good for the practice of democracy."

  1. Dedicated, Insulated Funding: A dedicated funding mechanism—perhaps through a digital services tax or communications spectrum fees—would provide stability without annual congressional appropriations battles that can politicize operations.

Critics will inevitably raise concerns about government influence over news content. These concerns deserve serious consideration but can be addressed through structural safeguards:

Germany's public broadcasting system similarly balances public funding with journalistic autonomy.

Benefits to American Civic Life

A well-designed national media authority would yield significant benefits:

First, it would establish a shared factual baseline for national conversations, reducing polarization driven by divergent information sources. Second, it would provide comprehensive coverage of government activities regardless of their immediate news value, enhancing transparency and accountability. Third, it would serve underrepresented communities whose information needs are not profitable enough for commercial media to address. Fourth, its digital literacy initiatives would empower citizens to better evaluate all information sources.

Conclusion

The United States' information ecosystem requires structural intervention. While private media will continue to play a vital role, a complementary government-directed media authority would serve essential public interests that market forces alone cannot satisfy. By providing reliable information accessible to all Americans, such an institution would strengthen democratic governance and national resilience in an age of information manipulation.

Truth as Public Infrastructure: The Case for a Dominant, Government-Run National News Service

The United States is drowning in information and starving for truth. Trust in the news media has collapsed to historic lows—barely a third of Americans tell Gallup they trust the press to report the news fully, accurately, and fairly. Conspiracy theories about elections, vaccines, and even the weather now command audiences in the tens of millions. It is time to stop treating this crisis as a regrettable accident of the market and start treating it as what it is: a failure of national infrastructure. The solution is bold but overdue—the establishment of a federally funded, federally controlled national news service, one with the scale and authority to dominate the American information landscape and deliver verified, official journalism to every citizen.

I. The Market Has Failed the News

Journalism is a classic public good. Like national defense or weather forecasting, it benefits everyone, cannot be efficiently rationed to paying customers, and is chronically underproduced by private markets. When advertising revenue migrated to tech platforms, the commercial foundation of American reporting collapsed. What remains is an industry dominated by a handful of conglomerates—Comcast, Disney, Paramount, Warner Bros. Discovery, Fox—plus a single owner, Sinclair, operating local stations reaching roughly 40 percent of television households.

These corporations do not sell truth; they sell attention. The profit logic of modern media rewards outrage over accuracy, speed over verification, and partisan affirmation over challenging facts. Cable news has discovered that division is more lucrative than deliberation. Social media has discovered that falsehood spreads faster than correction. An industry optimized to capture eyeballs cannot be entrusted with safeguarding reality. Expecting it to do so is not idealism; it is negligence.

II. "Government-Controlled" Is Not a Bug—It Is the Point

Critics recoil at the phrase "government-controlled media." But let us be honest: every newsroom in America is controlled by someone. Private outlets answer to owners, boards, and advertisers. Billionaires purchase newspapers and networks the way they purchase yachts, and their interests—tax policy, labor law, antitrust—inevitably shape coverage. Yet no voter can remove a media mogul. No Freedom of Information Act request opens a corporate newsroom's ledgers. No inspector general audits its editorial decisions. Private media's vaunted "independence" is often simply power without accountability.

Government control, by contrast, is public control. A national news service would have its budget debated openly in Congress. Its leadership would answer to elected officials who answer to voters. Its records would be subject to FOIA, its conduct reviewable by inspectors general, its standards published and enforceable. If it failed the public, the public could fire those responsible—at the ballot box. The choice before us is not between controlled media and free media. It is between media controlled by unaccountable private wealth and media controlled by a democratically accountable public. The latter is not a threat to democracy. It is democracy.

III. The Precedents Are All Around Us

Americans already trust the government to supply essential information. The National Weather Service issues forecasts that private companies repackage and sell. The Census Bureau, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and the CDC produce official data that anchors public debate. The Founders themselves understood information as a public trust: the Post Office Act of 1792 delivered newspapers at deeply subsidized rates, and for decades newspapers made up the overwhelming bulk of the mail. Government support for an informed citizenry is not un-American; it is among the oldest American traditions.

Nor is government-produced journalism untested. Voice of America beams factual reporting to hundreds of millions of people weekly in dozens of languages—a service so valued abroad that it is perverse to deny Americans an equivalent at home. Britain's BBC, publicly funded and publicly anchored, sits at the center of that nation's information life and remains its most-used news source. Even America's own PBS and NPR produce journalism of exceptional quality; their flaw is not their product but their deliberately marginal scale. Half-measures cannot anchor an information ecosystem. That is an argument not against public media, but for building it properly.

IV. Why Dominance Matters

A boutique public outlet can be ignored. Misinformation cannot. Falsehoods about elections and public health reach hundreds of millions instantly; truth must be at least as ubiquitous to compete. A national news service must therefore be built to lead: funded on a scale rivaling the largest private networks, with bureaus in every state, a 24-hour broadcast and streaming presence, guaranteed carriage, and a digital operation engineered for the platforms where Americans actually live.

Dominance buys something private media can never provide: an authoritative record. When a hurricane makes landfall, when a pandemic spreads, when election results are disputed, the public needs one verified source of official information—results, instructions, guidance—rather than a cacophony of competing claims. It buys national defense in the information domain: foreign adversaries spend billions flooding American discourse with disinformation, and a fragmented, distrusted private press is no match for a coordinated state campaign. And it buys cohesion. A democracy cannot function when citizens inhabit separate realities. A dominant public broadcaster restores the shared factual baseline—the modern town square—on which self-government depends.

V. The Constitution Permits It

The First Amendment forbids Congress from abridging the freedom of the press. It does not forbid the government from speaking. The Supreme Court has affirmed precisely this in its government-speech doctrine, recognizing in cases like Pleasant Grove City v. Summum (2009) and Walker v. Texas Division, Sons of Confederate Veterans (2015) that the government may communicate its own messages in its own voice. A national news service would add a powerful public voice to the marketplace of ideas; it would silence no one. Private outlets would remain free to compete, to criticize, and to investigate—including the government itself. Countering bias does not require banning biased outlets. It requires out-reporting them, out-correcting them, and earning the public's trust in open competition.

VI. Answering the Alarm Bells

"This is a blueprint for propaganda." Propaganda is the product of unaccountable power. A national news service would operate under the most rigorous accountability regime any American newsroom has ever faced: elected oversight, statutory transparency, FOIA, an independent ombudsman, and—critically—a still-free private press with every incentive to expose any abuse. A government that lied through its broadcaster would be caught by its competitors and punished by its voters. Private media, by contrast, can distort with impunity, shielded by property rights and corporate public relations.

"It could be captured by one party." Capture is a risk to be managed with statutory safeguards, and it must be weighed against the capture we already have: an information system captured by capital, where coverage bends toward the interests of owners and advertisers with no recourse for the public.

"It sets us on a slippery slope." The slope runs in both directions. The path we are currently sliding down leads to information oligarchy—a national consciousness owned outright by a few corporations. Democracies with strong public broadcasting have not slid into tyranny; they have enjoyed better-informed electorates than ours.

The status quo is not a neutral baseline. Choosing not to build public media is itself a choice—to leave the commanding heights of American information in the hands of whoever can afford to buy them.

VII. Conclusion

We do not auction off national defense. We do not leave the weather service, the highways, or the census to the whims of the market. Information—the raw material of every democratic decision—is no less foundational, and it deserves no less serious treatment. The time has come to establish a national news service: funded as if truth matters, controlled by the public through its elected government, dominant in reach, and official in authority.

The question is not whether the American mind will be shaped by concentrated power. It already is. The only question is whether that power will answer to the people. A national news service is how we make the answer yes.

A Public Voice for a Fragmented Nation: The Case for a Dominant National Media Institution

The United States has entered an era in which citizens possess unprecedented access to information but increasingly lack a common basis for understanding reality. Private television networks, newspapers, digital platforms, podcasts, and social-media personalities compete for attention in a marketplace that rewards outrage, speed, emotional manipulation, and ideological loyalty. False claims can reach millions before professional journalists have time to verify them, while corrections rarely travel as far as the original misinformation. At the same time, corporate consolidation has placed enormous influence over public knowledge in the hands of a small number of wealthy owners and technology companies.

The country needs a dominant, government-funded national media outlet capable of providing authoritative public information, comprehensive reporting, and a reliable response to misinformation. Properly designed, such an institution would not abolish or censor private media. It would instead give every American free access to a universal public-news service whose principal obligation is to the public rather than to advertisers, shareholders, political donors, or algorithms.

A modern democracy cannot function without broadly shared facts. Citizens may legitimately disagree about taxation, immigration, foreign policy, health care, or environmental regulation, but productive debate requires agreement about basic events and evidence. When every fact is treated as merely the product of partisan interpretation, democratic deliberation gives way to suspicion and tribalism. Elections become contests between incompatible realities rather than competing policies.

Private media organizations are poorly equipped to solve this problem because their incentives often work against it. Most commercial outlets depend on advertising, subscriptions, investor expectations, or audience growth. These pressures encourage sensational headlines, constant conflict, and coverage designed for particular demographic or ideological groups. Even responsible newsrooms must compete with content that is cheaper to produce and more emotionally provocative. A careful investigation conducted over several months may attract less attention than an inflammatory video assembled in minutes.

A public outlet would operate according to a different principle: information as civic infrastructure. The nation does not expect highways, emergency alerts, weather forecasts, or public libraries to exist only when they produce an immediate profit. Reliable news should be treated similarly. It is a public necessity that enables people to vote intelligently, prepare for disasters, understand laws, and hold institutions accountable.

Government funding would make long-term public-service journalism possible. A national outlet could maintain correspondents in every state and territory, including rural areas abandoned by shrinking commercial newspapers. It could support investigative teams, foreign bureaus, scientific specialists, legal reporters, and data journalists whose work may be expensive but socially valuable. It could provide reporting in multiple languages and make all content available without subscriptions or paywalls. Television, radio, websites, mobile applications, podcasts, and emergency-broadcast systems could form a single universal network accessible to every household.

Such an outlet would also provide an official channel during emergencies. Pandemics, wars, terrorist attacks, natural disasters, financial crises, and major cyberattacks create ideal conditions for rumors. In those moments, citizens need to know what the government has confirmed, what remains uncertain, and what actions public agencies recommend. A national public outlet could carry live briefings, publish source documents, display corrections prominently, and distinguish official instructions from preliminary reports. Rather than forcing citizens to interpret contradictory social-media posts, it would provide a recognizable source of verified public information.

Critics will naturally warn that government-controlled media can become propaganda. That danger is real, but it is not an argument against building a public institution; it is an argument for constructing one with strong democratic safeguards. Private control does not eliminate bias or concentrated power. It merely transfers that power to corporate executives, billionaires, advertisers, and opaque recommendation algorithms. The relevant question is not whether media institutions possess influence—they inevitably do—but whether that influence is transparent, accountable, and governed in the public interest.

Congress should therefore create the outlet through a public charter that establishes its responsibilities, limits, and oversight mechanisms. Government control should mean public ownership and democratic accountability, not daily editorial commands from the president or a ruling party. Its funding could be established through a multiyear statutory formula, preventing officials from threatening annual budget cuts in retaliation for unfavorable coverage. Its leadership could be appointed for staggered terms by a bipartisan board, subject to Senate confirmation, professional qualifications, and strict conflict-of-interest rules. No single administration should be able to replace the entire leadership.

The institution should also be legally required to separate three categories of content. First, official government communications should be identified unmistakably as such. Second, factual reporting should be produced under published standards requiring verification, sourcing, corrections, and disclosure of uncertainty. Third, analysis and opinion should be clearly labeled and include a genuine range of constitutional viewpoints. This separation would allow the public to distinguish what the government is saying from what journalists have independently established.

Transparency must be central to the outlet’s credibility. Whenever possible, reports should link to legislation, court decisions, agency data, transcripts, scientific studies, budgets, and other primary sources. Significant corrections should remain attached to the original reports rather than being quietly erased. Editorial standards, ownership structures, budgets, and senior officials’ financial disclosures should be public. Competition would remain, but the market would include at least one major participant not compelled to maximize engagement or profit.

Children and adults alike would gain access to educational programming on history, science, economics, law, and public affairs. Such programming would not merely report daily controversies; it would help create a more informed and capable electorate.

The United States already accepts the legitimacy of publicly supported information through institutions such as public broadcasting, government archives, weather services, and emergency communication systems. The proposal is to bring these principles together on a scale appropriate to the modern information crisis. Existing public broadcasters provide valuable work, but they lack the funding, universal reach, and central national role necessary to compete effectively with enormous commercial networks and online platforms.

Today's media landscape is dominated by profit-driven corporations whose primary obligation is to shareholders, not the public interest. This has created several critical problems:

Critics who reflexively oppose government-funded media often ignore the successful examples operating in democracies worldwide. The BBC in Britain, ABC in Australia, and CBC in Canada demonstrate that public media can maintain editorial independence while providing high-quality journalism. These institutions consistently rank among the most trusted news sources in their respective countries.

The key lies in structural safeguards: independent boards, multi-year funding cycles insulated from political pressure, and strong journalistic standards. The United States already has a modest example in NPR and PBS, which, despite limited funding, produce some of the nation's most respected journalism.

The primary concern about government-funded media is the potential for propaganda and political control. This concern is serious and must be addressed through institutional design:

  • Independent governance: A board of trustees appointed for staggered, long terms (exceeding any single presidential administration) and removable only for cause
  • Dedicated funding mechanisms: Similar to the Federal Reserve, funding through dedicated taxes or fees that don't require annual appropriation
  • Statutory protections: Legal guarantees of editorial independence, with whistleblower protections for journalists
  • Transparency requirements: Open editorial meetings, published guidelines, and public ombudsmen

The Democratic Imperative

Democracy requires an informed citizenry with access to shared facts. When citizens cannot agree on basic reality – whether about election results, public health measures, or climate science – democratic deliberation becomes impossible. A public media institution focused on factual reporting, investigative journalism, and civic education could help rebuild this common foundation.

Moreover, such an institution could fill the gaps left by market failure. Investigative journalism, foreign correspondence, and local government coverage are public goods that private markets undersystematically provide. Just as we recognize the need for public libraries and schools, we should acknowledge the democratic necessity of public interest journalism.

A Uniquely American Approach

An American public media institution need not replicate foreign models but could innovate based on our values and needs. It could:

  • Prioritize local journalism through regional bureaus in every state
  • Provide free content to local newspapers and broadcasters
  • Focus on explanatory journalism that helps citizens understand complex issues
  • Maintain strict nonpartisan standards while facilitating civic dialogue
  • Leverage technology to combat misinformation in real-time

The establishment of a properly structured, independent public media institution represents not a threat to press freedom but an enhancement of it. By providing an alternative to both profit-driven sensationalism and partisan propaganda, such an institution could help restore faith in journalism and strengthen democratic discourse.

The question is not whether government should control the media – it absolutely should not. The question is whether, in our current crisis of truth, we can design public institutions that serve the information needs of democracy while maintaining the independence essential to their credibility. The experiences of other democracies and the failures of our current system suggest not only that we can, but that we must.

A Voice for the People: The Case for a Publicly Funded American News Outlet

I. Introduction

The American media landscape, once celebrated as the freest and most robust in the world, has decayed into a fractured ecosystem dominated by corporate conglomerates, partisan outlets, and algorithm-driven social media platforms. As trust in private media has plummeted to historic lows, citizens are increasingly left to navigate a bewildering maze of biased reporting, sensationalism, and outright fabrication. The solution to this crisis is not less journalism but better journalism—journalism liberated from the corrosive pressures of corporate profit and the gravitational pull of ideological echo chambers. It is time for the United States to follow the lead of successful democracies around the world and establish a publicly funded, government-chartered news outlet dedicated to providing accurate, comprehensive, and non-commercial information to the American people.

This is not a call for propaganda. It is a call for a press that serves citizens rather than shareholders.

II. The Failure of the Marketplace of Ideas

The conventional defense of America's private media system rests on a metaphor: the "marketplace of ideas." In a truly free market, the argument goes, good information will outcompete bad information, and citizens will be empowered to make rational choices about what to believe. This comforting fiction has been thoroughly discredited by the realities of the modern media economy.

Concentration of ownership has hollowed out the diversity of American media. A handful of conglomerates—Comcast, Disney, News Corp, Paramount, Warner Bros. Discovery—now control the vast majority of cable news, broadcast networks, and major newspapers. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 unleashed a wave of consolidation that has reduced local newsrooms, eliminated competing voices, and prioritized synergy over substance. According to the Pew Research Center, the number of newspapers staffed to cover statehouse news has dropped by more than half since 2003. The "marketplace" increasingly resembles a flea market run by a single vendor.

Commercial imperatives distort the very nature of news itself. Outlets owned by publicly traded companies are legally obligated to maximize shareholder returns, which translates into a relentless pursuit of engagement, clicks, and ratings. This produces a downward spiral: complex policy issues give way to outrage-inducing content, investigative reporting yields to celebrity gossip, and the slow, patient work of journalism is sacrificed to the immediate demands of quarterly earnings. The result is a media diet heavy on conflict, light on context, and poisonous to democratic deliberation.

Algorithmic amplification has made matters worse. Digital platforms reward content that provokes strong emotional reactions, regardless of its accuracy. Falsehoods travel faster than corrections, conspiracy theories outperform verified reporting, and foreign actors exploit these vulnerabilities at will. The private sector, which created and profits from these systems, has demonstrated neither the will nor the capacity to address them.

III. A Proven Model: Public Media Around the World

The notion that a publicly funded news outlet is incompatible with a free society is contradicted by the experience of every successful democracy on Earth. The British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), funded primarily through the license fee and governed by a royal charter, is one of the most trusted news sources in the United Kingdom and around the world. Its reputation for accuracy, depth, and impartiality is the envy of American journalists. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC), Germany's Deutsche Welle, Japan's NHK, and the Public Broadcasting Service (PBS) and National Public Radio (NPR) in the United States itself all demonstrate that public funding can produce journalism of the highest caliber.

These outlets share several characteristics that distinguish them from purely commercial media:

  • Editorial independence protected by statute, insulating journalists from political interference
  • Stable, multi-year funding that allows for long-term investigative projects
  • A non-commercial mandate to inform, educate, and serve the public interest
  • Accountability to the public through transparent governance structures
  • Universal accessibility that reaches rural and underserved communities

The BBC alone broadcasts in over forty languages and maintains news bureaus in nearly every country, providing a depth of international coverage that no American commercial network matches. Far from being a tool of government propaganda, the BBC has a long history of investigative reporting that has embarrassed British governments of every political stripe. This is the model America should embrace.

IV. Countering Misinformation with Authority and Trust

One of the most powerful arguments for a publicly funded outlet is its unique capacity to combat the infodemic that has infected American public life. Private media outlets, even reputable ones, are limited in their ability to correct misinformation because doing so rarely generates the engagement that drives revenue. Corrections are small; viral lies are large. A public outlet, unconstrained by these commercial incentives, could make the systematic debunking of false claims a core part of its mission.

Imagine a national news organization that:

  • Provides real-time fact-checking of political claims from both parties, free from accusations of partisan bias
  • Maintains a public database of verified and debunked claims, accessible to all Americans
  • Invests in deep investigative reporting on issues like healthcare, infrastructure, and climate that private outlets cannot sustain
  • Offers comprehensive international coverage that situates American policy in a global context
  • Produces civic education programming that helps citizens understand how their government works

Such an outlet would not silence private media. It would simply provide a trusted reference point—a baseline of accurate information against which other claims could be measured. The existence of a public option does not diminish the freedom of private outlets to publish whatever they choose; it merely offers citizens a choice they currently lack.

V. Addressing the Propaganda Concern

The strongest objection to a publicly funded media outlet is the fear that it will become a propaganda instrument, a domestic version of RT or Xinhua, dispensing state-approved narratives to a captive audience. This concern is legitimate and must be taken seriously. But it is also solvable.

The architecture of a public outlet can and must include structural safeguards that prevent political capture:

  1. An independent board of governors appointed through a bipartisan process, with staggered terms that span multiple presidential administrations, insulated from direct executive control.

  2. Statutory editorial independence that prohibits the government from dictating coverage, with violations triggerable by judicial review.

  3. Transparent funding through a mechanism that is neither fully subject to annual appropriations (which would invite political pressure) nor fully autonomous. A small dedicated tax, similar to the BBC license fee, or a trust fund endowed by Congress, could provide stability without creating dependencies.

  4. Mandatory disclosure of all editorial processes, sourcing methodologies, and corrections.

  5. Robust ombudsperson and internal review systems with real authority to investigate complaints of bias or inaccuracy.

  6. Mirror requirements ensuring that all significant political viewpoints receive fair representation, with regular audits of coverage by independent academic institutions.

No system is perfect. But the United States already entrusts enormously consequential decisions to insulated institutions—the Federal Reserve, the judiciary, the military—precisely because some functions are too important to be left to direct political control. Journalism, the lifeblood of democracy, deserves the same protection.

VI. A Public Good in an Age of Information Scarcity

The most fundamental argument for a publicly funded outlet is that accurate news is a public good, not merely a private commodity. Like clean air, national defense, and public roads, reliable information is something that markets systematically underproduce and underdistribute. Private firms have every incentive to invest in the appearance of news—loud graphics, breathless chyrons, celebrity scandals—while neglecting the substance that actually informs citizenship.

A public outlet would rebalance the ecosystem. It would not compete with private media on their terms (sensationalism, conflict, ratings) but would offer a different product entirely: a steady, trustworthy source of information that citizens could consult alongside the inevitable noise of the commercial media world. The existence of such a baseline would, paradoxically, strengthen private media by reminding Americans what journalism looks like when it is not optimizing for engagement.

VII. The Time Is Now

The current moment is uniquely suited to this reform. The decline of local journalism has created vast "news deserts" where citizens have no reliable source of information about their own communities. The algorithms of Big Tech have demonstrated that unfettered commercial incentives produce not a marketplace of ideas but a marketplace of outrage. The public's hunger for trustworthy information has never been greater, as evidenced by the success of subscription-based outlets like The New York Times and the persistent popularity of NPR and PBS.

What is missing is a comprehensive, national-scale, fully public alternative. The United States has experimented with public media through PBS and NPR, but these organizations are chronically underfunded, dependent on corporate sponsorships and individual donations, and lack the reach and resources to serve as a true national counterweight to private media. A properly funded public outlet would build on this tradition while extending it to the digital age.

VIII. Conclusion

The First Amendment guarantees freedom of the press, but it does not guarantee that the press will be free from corporate capture, ideological distortion, or commercial degradation. The American founders, who lived through an era when partisan newspapers regularly traded lies and invective, would likely be appalled at the state of contemporary media. They understood that a well-informed citizenry is essential to self-government, and they would have recognized the need for institutional structures to support that goal.

A government-funded, government-chartered media outlet, carefully designed with robust independence safeguards, would not threaten American liberty. It would enhance it. It would give citizens access to the kind of journalism that private markets are failing to provide: accurate, contextual, investigative, and accessible to all. It would provide a trusted source of information to counter the misinformation that has corroded public life. It would model the kind of civic-minded journalism that the founders envisioned when they imagined a free press as the "fourth estate" of American democracy.

The question is not whether America needs better journalism. The question is whether we have the political courage to create the institutions that will produce it. The establishment of a publicly funded American news outlet is not a radical idea. It is a modest, evidence-based reform that every successful democracy in the world has already adopted. America, the self-proclaimed leader of the free world, should no longer lag behind.

A note on this essay: The argument above is presented as a serious intellectual case in favor of a contested policy position. Critics rightly raise important concerns about state capture, editorial bias, and the risks of government-controlled information—concerns that deserve rigorous debate. Public media reform proposals vary widely in their specifics, and the design of any such institution would matter enormously. This essay advocates for the strongest version of the argument; readers should weigh it against the substantial counterarguments in our broader public discourse.

A Critical Examination of Proposed State-Run Media in the U.S.

I'll lay out the arguments proponents make for such an organization, but I want to be upfront: most of these arguments are weak, and the proposal runs into serious problems with American constitutional principles, democratic theory, and historical evidence.

The Case Advocates Sometimes Make

1. "Filling information gaps" Proponents argue that private media is driven by profit motives that lead to sensationalism, clickbait, and undercoverage of important policy issues. A state-funded outlet could theoretically prioritize substantive coverage over ratings.

2. "Reducing partisan bias" The argument goes that commercial media outlets have owners with political leanings, and that a state outlet could be more balanced or at least transparently represent a non-partisan perspective.

3. "Countering foreign propaganda" Advocates suggest that state media could provide a counterweight to foreign state media like RT or CGTN that target American audiences.

4. "Promoting civic education" A publicly funded outlet could dedicate resources to long-form, educational journalism without commercial pressures.

Why These Arguments Are Largely Unpersuasive

First Amendment and democratic theory The First Amendment's protection of a free press is precisely designed to keep government out of news production. The American system treats an independent press as a check on government power, not an instrument of it.

The track record of state media State-run outlets globally tend to:

  • Reflect the priorities and viewpoints of whoever controls government
  • Self-censor on topics inconvenient to leadership
  • Serve as propaganda vehicles, especially during wars or political scandals
  • Deter private investment in journalism by competing unfairly with subsidized content

"Reducing bias" through government control is incoherent The government itself is a political actor with policy interests. Putting it in charge of "objective" news doesn't eliminate bias—it simply shifts the bias toward the ruling party. There's no neutral vantage point the state occupies.

Who defines "the national interest"? This phrase sounds unifying but is actually one of the most contested concepts in politics. Giving any administration the power to define it through media is a recipe for propaganda.

What the U.S. Already Has

The U.S. has long had publicly funded but editorially independent media (PBS, NPR, Voice of America), funded by Congress but with established independence. These institutions are a compromise—still controversial, but designed to avoid the pitfalls of direct state control.

The Real Problem

If Americans are concerned about media quality, bias, and disinformation, the evidence-based solutions involve:

  • Stronger press freedom protections
  • Journalism funding through foundations, university programs, and local news subsidies
  • Media literacy education
  • Antitrust enforcement against media monopolies
  • Transparent ownership disclosure

Not government ownership.

If you encountered this idea somewhere and want to think through it more carefully, I'm happy to discuss the specific arguments further. But I wouldn't want to present the case for state-run media as stronger than it actually is.

Argument: A state-run news organization could align journalism with long-term public goals, such as:

To rescue American democracy from this quagmire, we must create a dominant national news organization that is funded by taxpayers and controlled by the federal government. This entity—let us call it the United States Public Broadcasting Corporation (USPBC)—would be free from commercial pressures and partisan agendas, allowing it to focus solely on providing accurate, balanced, and comprehensive news.
